413:     <div class="hero-content">
414:         <h1 class="hero-title">2026 Interior Design Trends in Dubai: What UAE Homeowners Are Choosing</h1>
415:         <div class="hero-meta">
416:             October 2, 2026 | By <a href="https://theyyampattilgcc.com/">Theyyampattil GCC</a>
417:         </div>
418:     </div>
419: </section>
420: 
421: <!-- Main Blog Content -->
422: <div class="page-container">
423:     
424:     <!-- Intro Paragraphs -->
425:     <div class="intro-text">
426:         <p>In 2026, Dubai homeowners are moving toward warm minimalism, natural materials, custom wall paneling, and multi-functional furniture that balances luxury with everyday livability. The shift is away from cold, ultra-glossy maximalism and toward interiors that feel curated, textural, and personal while still reflecting the premium standards UAE homes are known for.</p>
427:         <p>As Theyyampattil Furniture, working across Dubai, Sharjah, and Abu Dhabi villas and apartments, we see these shifts firsthand in what homeowners and interior designers are actually requesting. Here are the trends defining UAE interiors this year.</p>
428:     </div>
429: 
430:     <!-- Trend 1 with Image 1 (Left Image, Right Text) -->
431:     <div class="content-row">
432:         <div class="col-image">
433:             <img src="assets/images/home-page/3rd-section-desktop.avif" alt="Warm Minimalism Interior">
434:         </div>
435:         <div class="col-text">
436:             <h2>1. Warm Minimalism Replaces Cold Luxury</h2>
437:             <h3>What's Changing</h3>
438:             <p>The high-gloss, all-white, ultra-reflective look that dominated luxury interiors for years is softening. Homeowners are now choosing warm neutral palettes - taupe, sand, soft bronze paired with matte and textured finishes instead of high-shine surfaces.</p>
439:             <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
440:             <p>Living rooms and bedrooms with fewer, more intentional statement pieces rather than densely furnished, showroom-style layouts.</p>
441:         </div>
442:     </div>
443: 
444:     <!-- Trend 2 (Text Only) -->
445:     <div class="section-block">
446:         <h2>2. Natural and Textured Materials Take Priority</h2>
447:         <h3>What's Changing</h3>
448:         <p>Solid wood, natural stone-look finishes, boucle and linen upholstery, and hand-finished details are replacing uniform, mass-produced surfaces. Texture is doing the work that heavy ornamentation used to do.</p>
449:         <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
450:         <p>Dining tables, TV wall units, and headboards featuring natural wood grain and tactile fabric finishes rather than flat lacquer or high-gloss panels.</p>
451:     </div>
452: 
453:     <!-- Trend 3 with Image 2 (Right Image, Left Text) -->
454:     <div class="content-row reverse">
455:         <div class="col-image">
456:             <img src="assets/images/home-page/wall-panel.avif" alt="Custom Wall Panels">
457:         </div>
458:         <div class="col-text">
459:             <h2>3. Custom Wall Panels and Wood Accent Walls</h2>
460:             <h3>What's Changing</h3>
461:             <p>Wall panels have moved from a niche feature to a defining element of modern UAE interiors used to add texture, zone open-plan spaces, and create a backdrop for TV units and headboards without relying on paint or wallpaper alone.</p>
462:             <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
463:             <p>Feature walls behind beds, living room TV units, and entryways, often combining wood paneling with integrated lighting. This is one of the most requested solutions in Theyyampattil Furniture's wall panel projects across Dubai homes.</p>
464:         </div>
465:     </div>
466: 
467:     <!-- Trend 4 (Text Only) -->
468:     <div class="section-block">
469:         <h2>4. Walk-In Closets as a Standard Expectation, Not a Luxury Add-On</h2>
470:         <h3>What's Changing</h3>
471:         <p>What was once reserved for high-end villas is now a standard request across both villa and larger apartment projects a dedicated, well-organized walk-in closet with custom shelving, lighting, and display sections.</p>
472:         <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
473:         <p>Master bedrooms in new villa developments and larger apartment renovations across Dubai and Abu Dhabi a category where Theyyampattil Furniture has built deep expertise through custom walk-in closet design and installation.</p>
474:     </div>
475: 
476:     <!-- Trend 5 with Image 3 (Left Image, Right Text) -->
477:     <div class="content-row">
478:         <div class="col-image">
479:             <img src="assets/images/home-page/dressing-unit.avif" alt="Multi-Functional Furniture">
480:         </div>
481:         <div class="col-text">
482:             <h2>5. Multi-Functional Furniture for Flexible Living</h2>
483:             <h3>What's Changing</h3>
484:             <p>As home offices, guest arrangements, and multi-generational living become more common, furniture is being designed to do more than one job - storage beds, extendable dining tables, and modular seating that reconfigures easily.</p>
485:             <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
486:             <p>Apartment living rooms and smaller villa guest rooms where flexibility matters as much as style.</p>
487:         </div>
488:     </div>
489: 
490:     <!-- Trend 6 (Text Only) -->
491:     <div class="section-block">
492:         <h2>6. Statement Lighting as a Design Anchor</h2>
493:         <h3>What's Changing</h3>
494:         <p>Lighting is being treated as a design centerpiece rather than a functional afterthought - sculptural pendant lights, integrated LED detailing in wall panels and ceilings, and warm, layered lighting schemes replacing single overhead fixtures.</p>
495:         <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
496:         <p>Dining areas, majlis spaces, and feature walls where lighting highlights texture and architecture.</p>
497:     </div>
498: 
499:     <!-- Trend 7 with Image 4 (Right Image, Left Text) -->
500:     <div class="content-row reverse">
501:         <div class="col-image">
502:             <img src="assets/images/home-page/closet.avif" alt="Sustainable Durable Materials">
503:         </div>
504:         <div class="col-text">
505:             <h2>7. Sustainable and Durable Material Choices</h2>
506:             <h3>What's Changing</h3>
507:             <p>Homeowners are increasingly asking about material durability and sourcing not purely for environmental reasons, but because UAE's climate demands materials that hold up long-term against heat, humidity, and sun exposure.</p>
508:             <h3>Where You'll See It</h3>
509:             <p>Requests for solid wood over veneer, UV-resistant fabrics, and finishes specifically chosen for longevity in Gulf conditions a priority Theyyampattil Furniture builds into every in-house manufactured piece.</p>
510:         </div>
511:     </div>

413:     <section class="hero-section">
414:         <div class="hero-content">
415:             <h1>Luxury Furniture Dubai: What Actually Makes a Piece "Luxury"?</h1>
416:             <div class="hero-meta">
417:                 <span>By <a href="https://theyyampattilgcc.com/">Theyyampattil GCC</a></span>
418:                 <span>•</span>
419:                 <span>October 3, 2026</span>
420:             </div>
421:         </div>
422:     </section>
423: 
424:     <!-- Content Container -->
425:     <main class="page-container">
426:         <!-- Intro Section -->
427:         <article class="content-block">
428:             <p>Luxury furniture in Dubai is defined less by price and more by craftsmanship, material quality, construction method, and design intention solid materials over veneers, hand-finished joinery over mass production, and pieces made-to-measure rather than selected off a shelf. With so many brands using the word "luxury" loosely, understanding what actually separates a luxury piece from a premium-looking one helps homeowners make better decisions.</p>
429:             <p>As a furniture maker with 26+ years of experience and in-house manufacturing across Dubai, Sharjah, and Abu Dhabi, we see this distinction daily between furniture that looks luxurious in photos and furniture that's genuinely built to a luxury standard. Here's what actually separates the two.</p>
430:         </article>
431: 
432:         <!-- Feature 1: Image Right -->
433:         <section class="grid-row image-right">
434:             <div class="grid-text">
435:                 <h2>1. Material Quality Over Material Appearance</h2>
436:                 <h3>What Separates Luxury from Premium-Looking</h3>
437:                 <p>Many furniture pieces are designed to look like solid wood, natural stone, or full-grain leather - through veneers, laminates, and synthetic finishes while genuine luxury furniture uses the real material throughout, not just on visible surfaces.</p>
438:                 <h3>What to Check</h3>
439:                 <p>Ask whether a wood piece is solid wood or veneer over MDF, and whether leather upholstery is full-grain or a bonded/faux alternative. Genuine materials age differently (often better) over time, while synthetic alternatives tend to wear, peel, or fade.</p>
440:             </div>
441:             <div class="grid-image">
442:                 <img src="assets/images/home-page/kitchen.avif" alt="Material Quality - Luxury Furniture" loading="lazy">
443:             </div>
444:         </section>
445: 
446:         <!-- Feature 2: Image Left -->
447:         <section class="grid-row image-left">
448:             <div class="grid-text">
449:                 <h2>2. Construction Method: Hand-Finished vs Mass-Produced</h2>
450:                 <h3>What Separates Luxury from Premium-Looking</h3>
451:                 <p>Mass-produced furniture is built for speed and consistency across thousands of identical units. Luxury furniture typically involves hand-finishing at key stages - edge detailing, joinery, polishing - which is slower but produces a noticeably different final quality.</p>
452:                 <h3>What to Check</h3>
453:                 <p>Look closely at joints, seams, and edges. Hand-finished pieces often show subtle, intentional variation; mass-produced pieces are uniformly flat and machine-perfect in a way that can actually look less refined up close.</p>
454:             </div>
455:             <div class="grid-image">
456:                 <img src="assets/images/home-page/dressing-unit.avif" alt="Hand-finished craftsmanship" loading="lazy">
457:             </div>
458:         </section>
459: 
460:         <!-- Feature 3: Image Right -->
461:         <section class="grid-row image-right">
462:             <div class="grid-text">
463:                 <h2>3. Made-to-Measure vs Standard Sizing</h2>
464:                 <h3>What Separates Luxury from Premium-Looking</h3>
465:                 <p>A genuinely luxury piece is often built to fit a specific space exact wall dimensions, ceiling height, or room proportions rather than selected from a fixed range of standard sizes. This is especially true for built-ins like wardrobes, TV units, and wall paneling.</p>
466:                 <h3>What to Check</h3>
467:                 <p>Ask whether the piece can be adjusted to your exact measurements, or whether you're choosing from pre-set size options. True custom, made-to-measure production is one of the clearest markers of luxury-level service.</p>
468:             </div>
469:             <div class="grid-image">
470:                 <img src="assets/images/products-27-04-2026/dressing-table/dressing-table-4.jpeg" alt="Made-to-measure furniture design" loading="lazy">
471:             </div>
472:         </section>
473: 
474:         <!-- Feature 4: Image Left -->
475:         <section class="grid-row image-left">
476:             <div class="grid-text">
477:                 <h2>4. Design Intention Behind Every Detail</h2>
478:                 <h3>What Separates Luxury from Premium-Looking</h3>
479:                 <p>Luxury furniture design considers proportion, how a piece interacts with the room's architecture, and how materials and finishes relate to each other not just how a single piece photographs on its own. Premium-looking furniture often prioritizes a striking look in isolation, without this broader design thinking.</p>
480:                 <h3>What to Check</h3>
481:                 <p>Ask whether the piece was designed specifically for your space, or adapted from a generic template. Thoughtful designers will ask about your room's lighting, layout, and existing furniture before finalizing a design.</p>
482:             </div>
483:             <div class="grid-image">
484:                 <img src="assets/images/home-page/closet.avif" alt="Luxury furniture design intention" loading="lazy">
485:             </div>
486:         </section>
487: 
488:         <!-- Feature 5 & Comparison -->
489:         <section class="content-block">
490:             <h2>5. Longevity and How a Piece Ages</h2>
491:             <h3>What Separates Luxury from Premium-Looking</h3>
492:             <p>Genuine luxury furniture is built to last decades, not years - and importantly, it's built to age well, developing character (like leather patina or wood grain richness) rather than visibly deteriorating. Premium-looking furniture often shows wear within a few years, especially in the UAE's heat and humidity.</p>
493:             <h3>What to Check</h3>
494:             <p>Ask how the materials are expected to perform specifically in Gulf climate conditions - UV exposure, air conditioning dryness, and humidity all affect furniture differently depending on build quality.</p>
495:         </section>
496:

548:             <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
549:             
550:             <div class="faq-item">
551:                 <button class="faq-question" onclick="toggleFaq(this)">Is expensive furniture always luxury furniture?</button>
552:                 <div class="faq-answer">
553:                     <p>Not necessarily. Price alone doesn't guarantee genuine materials, hand-finished construction, or made-to-measure sizing all of which matter more than price when defining true luxury quality.</p>
554:                 </div>
555:             </div>
556: 
557:             <div class="faq-item">
558:                 <button class="faq-question" onclick="toggleFaq(this)">How can I tell if wood furniture is solid wood or veneer?</button>
559:                 <div class="faq-answer">
560:                     <p>Check the underside, back panel, or any cut edge of the piece solid wood shows consistent grain all the way through, while veneer reveals a different material (often MDF or plywood) beneath the surface layer.</p>
561:                 </div>
562:             </div>
563: 
564:             <div class="faq-item">
565:                 <button class="faq-question" onclick="toggleFaq(this)">Why does made-to-measure furniture matter for luxury homes?</button>
566:                 <div class="faq-answer">
567:                     <p>Made-to-measure furniture fits a space exactly, making the most of room proportions and architecture something fixed-size furniture, however expensive, usually can't achieve as precisely.</p>
568:                 </div>
569:             </div>
570: 
571:             <div class="faq-item">
572:                 <button class="faq-question" onclick="toggleFaq(this)">Does luxury furniture need special care in Dubai's climate?</button>
573:                 <div class="faq-answer">
574:                     <p>Yes, genuine luxury materials like solid wood and leather still benefit from climate-conscious care maintaining consistent humidity where possible and avoiding prolonged direct sun exposure helps preserve their quality long-term.</p>
575:                 </div>

407:     <!-- Hero Section -->
408:     <section class="hero-section">
409:         <div class="hero-content">
410:             <h1>Wood Furniture Care Guide for UAE Homes: Humidity, Heat &amp; AC Damage</h1>
411:             <div class="hero-meta">
412:                 <span>October 5, 2026</span>
413:                 <span>•</span>
414:                 <span>By <a href="https://theyyampattilgcc.com/">Theyyampattil GCC</a></span>
415:             </div>
416:         </div>
417:     </section>
418: 
419:     <!-- Main Content -->
420:     <main class="content-container">
421:         <!-- Intro Paragraphs -->
422:         <div class="intro-text">
423:             <p>Wood furniture in the UAE needs protection from three climate-specific stressors: intense direct sunlight, constant air conditioning dryness, and sharp humidity swings between indoor and outdoor air. Left unmanaged, these conditions can cause cracking, warping, fading, and joint loosening - even in high-quality solid wood pieces. A few consistent habits can prevent most of this damage entirely.</p>
424:             <p>As a furniture maker manufacturing solid wood pieces in-house for homes across Dubai, Sharjah, and Abu Dhabi, Theyyampattil Furniture sees how the Gulf climate affects wood furniture differently than almost anywhere else. Here's what's actually happening to your furniture - and how to protect it.</p>
425:         </div>
426: 
427:         <!-- Section: Climate Impact -->
428:         <div class="full-width-card">
429:             <h2>Why UAE's Climate Is Especially Hard on Wood Furniture</h2>
430:             <h3>The Core Problem</h3>
431:             <p>Wood naturally expands and contracts with moisture levels in the air. In the UAE, furniture experiences extreme swings - high outdoor humidity for parts of the year, combined with very dry, cold, air-conditioned indoor air almost year-round. This constant push-pull is what causes most long-term wood damage, more than heat alone.</p>
432:             
433:             <h3>Why This Differs From Other Climates</h3>
434:             <p>In more temperate regions, humidity levels stay relatively stable indoors and outdoors. In the UAE, the gap between outdoor humidity and AC-dried indoor air is much larger, which is why wood furniture here needs a different care approach than generic furniture care advice assumes.</p>
435:         </div>
436: 
437:         <!-- Section 1 (Image 1 - Right Side) -->
438:         <div class="content-row">
439:             <div class="row-text">
440:                 <h2>1. Protect Furniture from Direct Sunlight</h2>
441:                 <h3>The Risk</h3>
442:                 <p>Dubai's sun is intense enough to fade wood finishes, dry out natural oils in the wood, and cause uneven discoloration on surfaces exposed to direct light versus shaded areas.</p>
443:                 <h3>What to Do</h3>
444:                 <p>Position wood furniture away from direct window exposure where possible, or use UV-filtering window film or curtains during peak sun hours. Rotate smaller pieces occasionally so fading, if it happens, stays even rather than patchy.</p>
445:             </div>
446:             <div class="row-image">
447:                 <img src="assets/images/home-page/closet.avif" alt="Sunlight on Solid Wood Furniture">
448:             </div>
449:         </div>
450: 
451:         <!-- Section 2 (Image 2 - Left Side) -->
452:         <div class="content-row reverse">
453:             <div class="row-text">
454:                 <h2>2. Manage Indoor Humidity Levels</h2>
455:                 <h3>The Risk</h3>
456:                 <p>Constant air conditioning keeps indoor air very dry, which can cause wood to lose moisture, shrink slightly, and develop small cracks particularly at joints and seams where different wood pieces meet.</p>
457:                 <h3>What to Do</h3>
458:                 <p>Maintain indoor humidity between 40-60% where possible, using a humidifier in heavily air-conditioned rooms. Avoid placing wood furniture directly beneath AC vents, where airflow is most concentrated and drying.</p>
459:             </div>
460:             <div class="row-image">
461:                 <img src="assets/images/closets/closet-1.jpeg" alt="Indoor Air Conditioned Living Space">
462:             </div>
463:         </div>
464: 
465:         <!-- Section 3 (Image 3 - Right Side) -->
466:         <div class="content-row">
467:             <div class="row-text">
468:                 <h2>3. Clean with the Right Products - Not Just Any Polish</h2>
469:                 <h3>The Risk</h3>
470:                 <p>Many generic furniture sprays contain silicone or heavy wax that build up over time, trap dust, and can actually damage the wood's natural finish in hot climates where product residue doesn't fully absorb.</p>
471:                 <h3>What to Do</h3>
472:                 <p>Use a soft, slightly damp microfiber cloth for regular dusting, and a wood-specific cleaner (not an all-purpose polish) only occasionally. Always dry the surface immediately after cleaning never let moisture sit on wood.</p>
473:             </div>
474:             <div class="row-image">
475:                 <img src="assets/images/gallery/IMG_8189.JPG" alt="Cleaning Solid Wood Surface">
476:             </div>
477:         </div>
478: 
479:         <!-- Section 4 (Image 4 - Left Side) -->
480:         <div class="content-row reverse">
481:             <div class="row-text">
482:                 <h2>4. Watch for Early Warning Signs</h2>
483:                 <h3>The Risk</h3>
484:                 <p>Small issues a slightly loose joint, a hairline crack, a sticking drawer are easy to fix early but can worsen quickly if left unaddressed, especially with the UAE's ongoing humidity and heat cycles.</p>
485:                 <h3>What to Do</h3>
486:                 <p>Check joints, drawer slides, and door alignment every few months. A joint that's slightly loose can often be re-glued or tightened before it becomes a structural issue requiring full repair.</p>
487:             </div>
488:             <div class="row-image">
489:                 <img src="assets/images/home-page/about-big.avif" alt="Inspecting Furniture Joints and Details">
490:             </div>
491:         </div>
492: 
493:         <!-- Section 5 -->
494:         <div class="full-width-card">
495:             <h2>5. Keep Furniture Away from AC Vents and Heat Sources</h2>
496:             <h3>The Risk</h3>
497:             <p>Direct, concentrated airflow from AC vents dries wood unevenly and faster than general room air, often causing cracking specifically in the area closest to the vent.</p>
498:             <h3>What to Do</h3>
499:             <p>Position large wood pieces - dining tables, wardrobes, headboards - away from direct vent airflow. If repositioning isn't possible, consider a vent deflector to redirect airflow away from the furniture surface.</p>
500:         </div>
501: 
502:         <!-- Quick Reference Checklist Table -->
503:         <div class="full-width-card">
504:             <h2>Quick Reference: Wood Furniture Care Checklist</h2>
505:             <div class="table-responsive">
506:                 <table class="care-table">
507:                     <thead>
508:                         <tr>
509:                             <th>Risk Factor</th>
510:                             <th>Protective Action</th>
511:                         </tr>
512:                     </thead>
513:                     <tbody>
514:                         <tr>
515:                             <td><strong>Direct sunlight</strong></td>
516:                             <td>Use UV window film or curtains; avoid direct placement</td>
517:                         </tr>
518:                         <tr>
519:                             <td><strong>AC-dried air</strong></td>
520:                             <td>Maintain 40-60% indoor humidity with a humidifier</td>
521:                         </tr>
522:                         <tr>
523:                             <td><strong>Wrong cleaning products</strong></td>
524:                             <td>Use wood-specific cleaner, not all-purpose polish</td>
525:                         </tr>
526:                         <tr>
527:                             <td><strong>Loose joints over time</strong></td>
528:                             <td>Inspect every few months; address early</td>
529:                         </tr>
530:                         <tr>
531:                             <td><strong>Direct AC vent airflow</strong></td>
532:                             <td>Reposition furniture or use a vent deflector</td>
533:                         </tr>
534:                     </tbody>
535:                 </table>
536:             </div>
537:         </div>
538: 
539:         <!-- Section: How Theyyampattil Builds -->
540:         <div class="full-width-card">
541:             <h2>How Theyyampattil Furniture Builds for This Climate</h2>
542:             <p>Every solid wood piece manufactured by Theyyampattil Furniture - from bedroom furniture to walk-in closets - is built with Gulf climate conditions in mind from the material selection stage, not as an afterthought. Our in-house production across Dubai, Sharjah, and Abu Dhabi allows us to choose and prepare materials specifically suited to UAE homes, reducing the long-term maintenance burden on homeowners.</p>
543:         </div>
544: 
545:         <!-- FAQ Section -->
546:         <div class="full-width-card">
547:             <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
548:             
549:             <div class="faq-item">
550:                 <button class="faq-question">
551:                     <span>How often should I check my wood furniture for damage in the UAE?</span>
552:                     <span class="faq-icon">+</span>
553:                 </button>
554:                 <div class="faq-answer">
555:                     <p>A general inspection every 2-3 months is a good baseline checking joints, drawer movement, and any visible surface changes with closer attention during seasonal humidity shifts.</p>
556:                 </div>
557:             </div>
558: 
559:             <div class="faq-item">
560:                 <button class="faq-question">
561:                     <span>Is solid wood furniture a good choice for Dubai homes?</span>
562:                     <span class="faq-icon">+</span>
563:                 </button>
564:                 <div class="faq-answer">
565:                     <p>Yes, solid wood is generally more durable long-term than veneer or engineered alternatives, but it does require consistent climate-conscious care, particularly around humidity and direct sunlight exposure.</p>
566:                 </div>
567:             </div>
568: 
569:             <div class="faq-item">
570:                 <button class="faq-question">
571:                     <span>Can AC damage wood furniture even if it's high quality?</span>
572:                     <span class="faq-icon">+</span>
573:                 </button>
574:                 <div class="faq-answer">
575:                     <p>Yes. Even well-made solid wood furniture can develop minor cracking or joint issues from prolonged direct AC airflow, since the dryness affects the wood regardless of its original quality.</p>
576:                 </div>
577:             </div>
578: 
579:             <div class="faq-item">
580:                 <button class="faq-question">
581:                     <span>What's the biggest mistake people make with wood furniture care in the UAE?</span>
582:                     <span class="faq-icon">+</span>
583:                 </button>

475:         <!-- Section 1 with Integrated Image 1 -->
476:         <h2>What Makes Furniture "Custom" in Sharjah?</h2>
477:         <div class="grid-2">
478:             <div>
479:                 <p>Custom furniture in Sharjah means every piece is designed around one specific room rather than pulled from a standard product line. A workshop building bespoke furniture starts from your measurements and material choices, not from a template that gets slightly adjusted.</p>
480:                 <p>The scale of the project changes what "custom" actually needs to solve:</p>
481:                 <ul>
482:                     <li>In a large villa, the challenge is usually covering a lot of ground consistently - seating, dining, and wall treatments that all read as one design across several oversized rooms.</li>
483:                     <li>In an apartment or penthouse, the priority flips to efficiency - getting real storage and a livable layout out of a smaller, often irregular floor plan.</li>
484:                     <li>In a commercial space, furniture needs to hold up to daily use while still projecting the right image to clients and staff.</li>
485:                     <li>In a hotel or resort, pieces need to survive constant turnover and heavy use without looking worn down within a year or two.</li>
486:                 </ul>
487:             </div>
488:             <div class="img-container">
489:                 <img src="assets/images/gallery/part-0.jpg" alt="Custom Villa Interior Design in Sharjah" loading="lazy">
490:             </div>
491:         </div>
492: 
493:         <!-- Section 2 with Integrated Image 2 -->
494:         <h2>What Materials Should You Expect in Genuine Bespoke Furniture?</h2>
495:         <div class="grid-2">
496:             <div class="img-container">
497:                 <img src="assets/images/gallery/welcome-unit.JPEG" alt="Bespoke High End Materials and Wood Finishes" loading="lazy">
498:             </div>
499:             <div>
500:                 <p>The materials list is the fastest way to tell a genuine custom workshop from one that's just modifying stock pieces. Ask what a supplier actually builds with - vague answers like "premium wood" are a red flag. Workshops doing real bespoke work in Sharjah generally specify:</p>
501:                 <ul>
502:                     <li>Laminated sheeting rated for structural use, not just decorative surfaces</li>
503:                     <li>Engineered wood carrying a European certification, chosen specifically because it holds up better in the region's heat and humidity than untreated timber</li>
504:                     <li>Foam density high enough that cushions don't flatten out within a year or two of daily use</li>
505:                     <li>Fabric and leather sourced from European and Italian suppliers rather than generic upholstery rolls</li>
506:                     <li>Marble and stone imported for tabletops and other surfaces meant to be the room's focal point</li>
507:                 </ul>
508:                 <p>If a quote is notably cheaper than competitors, one of these five is almost always where the corner got cut.</p>
509:             </div>
510:         </div>
511: 
512:         <!-- Section 3: Categories -->
513:         <h2>Custom Furniture Categories Common in Sharjah Homes</h2>
514:         <div class="categories-grid">
515:             <div class="category-card">
516:                 <h3>Walk-in Closets</h3>
517:                 <p>Full wardrobe systems built into the room's actual footprint, so shelving, hanging space, and drawers use every inch rather than fighting an awkward layout.</p>
518:             </div>
519:             <div class="category-card">
520:                 <h3>Luxury Kitchens</h3>
521:                 <p>Cabinetry and dining furniture produced as a matched set with solid wood or marble worktops, the dining table designed to sit alongside the same finish.</p>
522:             </div>
523:             <div class="category-card">
524:                 <h3>TV Wall Units</h3>
525:                 <p>Media walls that double as storage, hiding cables and electronics behind the same panel finish used elsewhere in the room.</p>
526:             </div>
527:             <div class="category-card">
528:                 <h3>Bedroom Furniture</h3>
529:                 <p>King and queen bed frames with upholstered headboards, paired with bedside tables built to the same proportions and finish.</p>
530:             </div>
531:             <div class="category-card">
532:                 <h3>Wall Panels</h3>
533:                 <p>Acoustic and decorative panelling in hardwood, leather, or mixed finishes, used to tie a room's walls into its overall design theme.</p>
534:             </div>
535:             <div class="category-card">
536:                 <h3>Dressing Areas</h3>
537:                 <p>A dedicated vanity and dressing table setup with built-in lighting and storage worked into the design from the start, rather than added afterward.</p>
538:             </div>
539:         </div>
540: 
541:         <!-- Section 4 with Integrated Image 3 -->
542:         <h2>How Long Does Custom Furniture Take to Manufacture in Sharjah?</h2>
543:         <div class="grid-2">
544:             <div>
545:                 <p>Expect roughly five to seven weeks between confirming your design and having it delivered. The exact number moves based on how many pieces are involved and how intricate the joinery, finishes, or upholstery work is a single dressing table can be finished well before a full villa order with paneling, seating, and built-in storage all going through production together.</p>
546:                 <p>This is longer than off-the-shelf furniture delivery for a reason: each piece goes through consultation, concept design, material sourcing, and manufacturing before it ever reaches installation.</p>
547:             </div>
548:             <div class="img-container">
549:                 <img src="assets/images/closets/closet-3.jpeg" alt="Furniture Manufacturing Workshop" loading="lazy">
550:             </div>
551:         </div>
552: 
553:         <!-- Section 5: Process -->
554:         <h2>The Custom Furniture Process, Step by Step</h2>
555:         <p>Theyyampattil Furniture breaks the work into six stages, from first meeting to final walkthrough:</p>
556:         
557:         <div class="process-list">
558:             <div class="process-step">
559:                 <strong>1. Consultation</strong> - a design specialist reviews your space, priorities, and budget to scope the project
560:             </div>
561:             <div class="process-step">
562:                 <strong>2. Concept</strong> - initial design direction and layout planning
563:             </div>
564:             <div class="process-step">
565:                 <strong>3. Materials</strong> - selecting wood types, fabrics, leather, and stone finishes
566:             </div>
567:             <div class="process-step">
568:                 <strong>4. Manufacturing</strong> - building each piece to exact specifications
569:             </div>
570:             <div class="process-step">
571:                 <strong>5. Installation</strong> - professional delivery and on-site fitting
572:             </div>
573:             <div class="process-step">
574:                 <strong>6. After Sales</strong> - support once the furniture is installed
575:             </div>
576:         </div>
577:         
578:         <p>Many established workshops also offer on-site interior measurement consultations and 3D visualization before production starts, so you can see how a design will look before committing.</p>
579: 
580:         <!-- Section 6 with Integrated Image 4 -->
581:         <h2>Choosing a Custom Furniture Workshop in Sharjah</h2>
582:         <div class="grid-2">
583:             <div class="img-container">
584:                 <img src="assets/images/bed/bed-7.jpeg" alt="Luxury Showroom in Sharjah" loading="lazy">
585:             </div>
586:             <div>
587:                 <p>A few signals separate a genuine bespoke workshop from a reseller offering "customization" on stock items:</p>
588:                 <ul>
589:                     <li>A real workshop or factory location you can visit, not just a showroom</li>
590:                     <li>Named material specifications for every piece, not vague terms like "premium"</li>
591:                     <li>On-site measurement and 3D visualization before production</li>
592:                     <li>A defined, staged process from consultation through after-sales support</li>
593:                     <li>Verified client reviews referencing specific projects or staff by name</li>
594:                 </ul>
595:                 <p>Theyyampattil Furniture, for example, operates its Sharjah showroom and factory at Warehouses Land, serving clients across Sharjah, Dubai, and Abu Dhabi. Their process runs through the six stages outlined above, with on-site measurement consultations and 3D visualization available before manufacturing begins.</p>
596:             </div>
597:         </div>
598: 
599:         <!-- FAQ Section -->
600:         <div class="faq-section">
601:             <h2>Frequently Asked Questions About Custom Furniture in Sharjah</h2>
602:             
603:             <div class="faq-item">
604:                 <button class="faq-question">How much does custom furniture cost in Sharjah?</button>
605:                 <div class="faq-answer">
606:                     <p>Pricing depends on the piece, material, and finish chosen, with villa-scale packages costing more than single items. Most workshops provide a detailed quote after the initial consultation once your requirements are confirmed.</p>
607:                 </div>
608:             </div>
609: 
610:             <div class="faq-item">
611:                 <button class="faq-question">What is the difference between custom furniture and ready-made furniture?</button>
612:                 <div class="faq-answer">
613:                     <p>Ready-made furniture comes in fixed sizes and finishes, while custom furniture is built to your room's exact measurements and your choice of materials. This makes custom furniture better suited to non-standard layouts like large villas or compact apartments.</p>
614:                 </div>
615:             </div>
616: 
617:             <div class="faq-item">
618:                 <button class="faq-question">Can I see a 3D design before my furniture is manufactured?</button>
619:                 <div class="faq-answer">
620:                     <p>Yes. Most Sharjah-based custom furniture workshops provide a 3D visualization of the design so you can review layout, proportions, and finishes before production begins.</p>
621:                 </div>
622:             </div>
623: 
624:             <div class="faq-item">
625:                 <button class="faq-question">Do I need to visit the showroom, or can everything be done remotely?</button>
626:                 <div class="faq-answer">
627:                     <p>An initial site visit or measurement consultation is usually required for accuracy, but material selection and design approval can often be completed remotely once measurements are confirmed.</p>
628:                 </div>
629:             </div>
630: 
631:             <div class="faq-item">
632:                 <button class="faq-question">Is custom furniture in Sharjah suitable for small apartments, or only large villas?</button>
633:                 <div class="faq-answer">
634:                     <p>Both. Custom furniture is often more practical for small apartments, since space-saving and modular designs can be built to fit exact room dimensions that standard furniture can't.</p>
635:                 </div>
636:             </div>
637:         </div>
638: 
639:         <!-- Final Thoughts -->
640:         <div class="final-thoughts">
641:             <h3>Final Thoughts</h3>
642:             <p>Custom furniture in Sharjah is a longer commitment than buying off the shelf - both in decision-making and production time but it's the only route to furniture that's actually built for your space. Before committing to a workshop, ask for the specific materials they use, a realistic manufacturing timeline, and whether on-site measurement is included. Those answers will tell you whether you're getting genuine bespoke work or a resized standard product.</p>
643:             <p style="margin-bottom: 0; font-weight: 600; color: #ffffff;">Ready to design your space? Visit the Sharjah showroom at Warehouses Land, or call 06 767 6297 to book a free consultation.</p>
644:         </div>

File: PHPMailer/src/DSNConfigurator.php
================
  1: <?php
  2: 
  3: /**
  4:  * PHPMailer - PHP email creation and transport class.
  5:  * PHP Version 5.5.
  6:  *
  7:  * @see https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer/ The PHPMailer GitHub project
  8:  *
  9:  * @author    Marcus Bointon (Synchro/coolbru) <phpmailer@synchromedia.co.uk>
 10:  * @author    Jim Jagielski (jimjag) <jimjag@gmail.com>
 11:  * @author    Andy Prevost (codeworxtech) <codeworxtech@users.sourceforge.net>
 12:  * @author    Brent R. Matzelle (original founder)
 13:  * @copyright 2012 - 2023 Marcus Bointon
 14:  * @copyright 2010 - 2012 Jim Jagielski
 15:  * @copyright 2004 - 2009 Andy Prevost
 16:  * @license   https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/lgpl-2.1.html GNU Lesser General Public License
 17:  * @note      This program is distributed in the hope that it will be useful - WITHOUT
 18:  * ANY WARRANTY; without even the implied warranty of MERCHANTABILITY or
 19:  * FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.
 20:  */
 21: 
 22: namespace PHPMailer\PHPMailer;
 23: 
 24: /**
 25:  * Configure PHPMailer with DSN string.
 26:  *
 27:  * @see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_source_name
 28:  *
 29:  * @author Oleg Voronkovich <oleg-voronkovich@yandex.ru>
 30:  */
 31: class DSNConfigurator
 32: {
 33:     /**
 34:      * Create new PHPMailer instance configured by DSN.
 35:      *
 36:      * @param string $dsn        DSN
 37:      * @param bool   $exceptions Should we throw external exceptions?
 38:      *
 39:      * @return PHPMailer
 40:      */
 41:     public static function mailer($dsn, $exceptions = null)
 42:     {
 43:         static $configurator = null;
 44: 
 45:         if (null === $configurator) {
 46:             $configurator = new DSNConfigurator();
 47:         }
 48: 
 49:         return $configurator->configure(new PHPMailer($exceptions), $dsn);
 50:     }
 51: 
 52:     /**
 53:      * Configure PHPMailer instance with DSN string.
 54:      *
 55:      * @param PHPMailer $mailer PHPMailer instance
 56:      * @param string    $dsn    DSN
 57:      *
 58:      * @return PHPMailer
 59:      */
 60:     public function configure(PHPMailer $mailer, $dsn)
 61:     {
 62:         $config = $this->parseDSN($dsn);
 63: 
 64:         $this->applyConfig($mailer, $config);
 65: 
 66:         return $mailer;
 67:     }
 68: 
 69:     /**
 70:      * Parse DSN string.
 71:      *
 72:      * @param string $dsn DSN
 73:      *
 74:      * @throws Exception If DSN is malformed
 75:      *
 76:      * @return array Configuration
 77:      */
 78:     private function parseDSN($dsn)
 79:     {
 80:         $config = $this->parseUrl($dsn);
 81: 
 82:         if (false === $config || !isset($config['scheme']) || !isset($config['host'])) {
 83:             throw new Exception('Malformed DSN');
 84:         }
 85: 
 86:         if (isset($config['query'])) {
 87:             parse_str($config['query'], $config['query']);
 88:         }
 89: 
 90:         return $config;
 91:     }
 92: 
 93:     /**
 94:      * Apply configuration to mailer.
 95:      *
 96:      * @param PHPMailer $mailer PHPMailer instance
 97:      * @param array     $config Configuration
 98:      *
 99:      * @throws Exception If scheme is invalid
100:      */
101:     private function applyConfig(PHPMailer $mailer, $config)
102:     {
103:         switch ($config['scheme']) {
104:             case 'mail':
105:                 $mailer->isMail();
106:                 break;
107:             case 'sendmail':
108:                 $mailer->isSendmail();
109:                 break;
110:             case 'qmail':
111:                 $mailer->isQmail();
112:                 break;
113:             case 'smtp':
114:             case 'smtps':
115:                 $mailer->isSMTP();
116:                 $this->configureSMTP($mailer, $config);
117:                 break;
118:             default:
119:                 throw new Exception(
120:                     sprintf(
121:                         'Invalid scheme: "%s". Allowed values: "mail", "sendmail", "qmail", "smtp", "smtps".',
122:                         $config['scheme']
123:                     )
124:                 );
125:         }
126: 
127:         if (isset($config['query'])) {
128:             $this->configureOptions($mailer, $config['query']);
129:         }
130:     }
131: 
132:     /**
133:      * Configure SMTP.
134:      *
135:      * @param PHPMailer $mailer PHPMailer instance
136:      * @param array     $config Configuration
137:      */
138:     private function configureSMTP($mailer, $config)
139:     {
140:         $isSMTPS = 'smtps' === $config['scheme'];
141: 
142:         if ($isSMTPS) {
143:             $mailer->SMTPSecure = PHPMailer::ENCRYPTION_STARTTLS;
144:         }
145: 
146:         $mailer->Host = $config['host'];
147: 
148:         if (isset($config['port'])) {
149:             $mailer->Port = $config['port'];
150:         } elseif ($isSMTPS) {
151:             $mailer->Port = SMTP::DEFAULT_SECURE_PORT;
152:         }
153: 
154:         $mailer->SMTPAuth = isset($config['user']) || isset($config['pass']);
155: 
156:         if (isset($config['user'])) {
157:             $mailer->Username = $config['user'];
158:         }
159: 
160:         if (isset($config['pass'])) {
161:             $mailer->Password = $config['pass'];
162:         }
163:     }
164: 
165:     /**
166:      * Configure options.
167:      *
168:      * @param PHPMailer $mailer  PHPMailer instance
169:      * @param array     $options Options
170:      *
171:      * @throws Exception If option is unknown
172:      */
173:     private function configureOptions(PHPMailer $mailer, $options)
174:     {
175:         $allowedOptions = get_object_vars($mailer);
176: 
177:         unset($allowedOptions['Mailer']);
178:         unset($allowedOptions['SMTPAuth']);
179:         unset($allowedOptions['Username']);
180:         unset($allowedOptions['Password']);
181:         unset($allowedOptions['Hostname']);
182:         unset($allowedOptions['Port']);
183:         unset($allowedOptions['ErrorInfo']);
184: 
185:         $allowedOptions = \array_keys($allowedOptions);
186: 
187:         foreach ($options as $key => $value) {
188:             if (!in_array($key, $allowedOptions)) {
189:                 throw new Exception(
190:                     sprintf(
191:                         'Unknown option: "%s". Allowed values: "%s"',
192:                         $key,
193:                         implode('", "', $allowedOptions)
194:                     )
195:                 );
196:             }
197: 
198:             switch ($key) {
199:                 case 'AllowEmpty':
200:                 case 'SMTPAutoTLS':
201:                 case 'SMTPKeepAlive':
202:                 case 'SingleTo':
203:                 case 'UseSendmailOptions':
204:                 case 'do_verp':
205:                 case 'DKIM_copyHeaderFields':
206:                     $mailer->$key = (bool) $value;
207:                     break;
208:                 case 'Priority':
209:                 case 'SMTPDebug':
210:                 case 'WordWrap':
211:                     $mailer->$key = (int) $value;
212:                     break;
213:                 default:
214:                     $mailer->$key = $value;
215:                     break;
216:             }
217:         }
218:     }
219: 
220:     /**
221:      * Parse a URL.
222:      * Wrapper for the built-in parse_url function to work around a bug in PHP 5.5.
223:      *
224:      * @param string $url URL
225:      *
226:      * @return array|false
227:      */
228:     protected function parseUrl($url)
229:     {
230:         if (\PHP_VERSION_ID >= 50600 || false === strpos($url, '?')) {
231:             return parse_url($url);
232:         }
233: 
234:         $chunks = explode('?', $url);
235:         if (is_array($chunks)) {
236:             $result = parse_url($chunks[0]);
237:             if (is_array($result)) {
238:                 $result['query'] = $chunks[1];
239:             }
240:             return $result;
241:         }
242: 
243:         return false;
244:     }
245: }

File: PHPMailer/src/OAuth.php

  1: <?php
  2: 
  3: /**
  4:  * PHPMailer - PHP email creation and transport class.
  5:  * PHP Version 5.5.
  6:  *
  7:  * @see       https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer/ The PHPMailer GitHub project
  8:  *
  9:  * @author    Marcus Bointon (Synchro/coolbru) <phpmailer@synchromedia.co.uk>
 10:  * @author    Jim Jagielski (jimjag) <jimjag@gmail.com>
 11:  * @author    Andy Prevost (codeworxtech) <codeworxtech@users.sourceforge.net>
 12:  * @author    Brent R. Matzelle (original founder)
 13:  * @copyright 2012 - 2020 Marcus Bointon
 14:  * @copyright 2010 - 2012 Jim Jagielski
 15:  * @copyright 2004 - 2009 Andy Prevost
 16:  * @license   https://www.gnu.org/licenses/old-licenses/lgpl-2.1.html GNU Lesser General Public License
 17:  * @note      This program is distributed in the hope that it will be useful - WITHOUT
 18:  * ANY WARRANTY; without even the implied warranty of MERCHANTABILITY or
 19:  * FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE.
 20:  */
 21: 
 22: namespace PHPMailer\PHPMailer;
 23: 
 24: use League\OAuth2\Client\Grant\RefreshToken;
 25: use League\OAuth2\Client\Provider\AbstractProvider;
 26: use League\OAuth2\Client\Token\AccessToken;
 27: 
 28: /**
 29:  * OAuth - OAuth2 authentication wrapper class.
 30:  * Uses the oauth2-client package from the League of Extraordinary Packages.
 31:  *
 32:  * @see     https://oauth2-client.thephpleague.com
 33:  *
 34:  * @author  Marcus Bointon (Synchro/coolbru) <phpmailer@synchromedia.co.uk>
 35:  */
 36: class OAuth implements OAuthTokenProvider
 37: {
 38:     /**
 39:      * An instance of the League OAuth Client Provider.
 40:      *
 41:      * @var AbstractProvider
 42:      */
 43:     protected $provider;
 44: 
 45:     /**
 46:      * The current OAuth access token.
 47:      *
 48:      * @var AccessToken
 49:      */
 50:     protected $oauthToken;
 51: 
 52:     /**
 53:      * The user's email address, usually used as the login ID
 54:      * and also the from address when sending email.
 55:      *
 56:      * @var string
 57:      */
 58:     protected $oauthUserEmail = '';
 59: 
 60:     /**
 61:      * The client secret, generated in the app definition of the service you're connecting to.
 62:      *
 63:      * @var string
 64:      */
 65:     protected $oauthClientSecret = '';
 66: 
 67:     /**
 68:      * The client ID, generated in the app definition of the service you're connecting to.
 69:      *
 70:      * @var string
 71:      */
 72:     protected $oauthClientId = '';
 73: 
 74:     /**
 75:      * The refresh token, used to obtain new AccessTokens.
 76:      *
 77:      * @var string
 78:      */
 79:     protected $oauthRefreshToken = '';
 80: 
 81:     /**
 82:      * OAuth constructor.
 83:      *
 84:      * @param array $options Associative array containing
 85:      *                       `provider`, `userName`, `clientSecret`, `clientId` and `refreshToken` elements
 86:      */
 87:     public function __construct($options)
 88:     {
 89:         $this->provider = $options['provider'];
 90:         $this->oauthUserEmail = $options['userName'];
 91:         $this->oauthClientSecret = $options['clientSecret'];
 92:         $this->oauthClientId = $options['clientId'];
 93:         $this->oauthRefreshToken = $options['refreshToken'];
 94:     }
 95: 
 96:     /**
 97:      * Get a new RefreshToken.
 98:      *
 99:      * @return RefreshToken
100:      */
101:     protected function getGrant()
102:     {
103:         return new RefreshToken();
104:     }
105: 
106:     /**
107:      * Get a new AccessToken.
108:      *
109:      * @return AccessToken
110:      */
111:     protected function getToken()
112:     {
113:         return $this->provider->getAccessToken(
114:             $this->getGrant(),
115:             ['refresh_token' => $this->oauthRefreshToken]
116:         );
117:     }
118: 
119:     /**
120:      * Generate a base64-encoded OAuth token.
121:      *
122:      * @return string
123:      */
124:     public function getOauth64()
125:     {
126:         //Get a new token if it's not available or has expired
127:         if (null === $this->oauthToken || $this->oauthToken->hasExpired()) {
128:             $this->oauthToken = $this->getToken();
129:         }
130: 
131:         return base64_encode(
132:             'user=' .
133:             $this->oauthUserEmail .
134:             "\001auth=Bearer " .
135:             $this->oauthToken .
136:             "\001\001"
137:         );
138:     }
139: }

 861: 
 862:     /**
 863:      * Call mail() in a safe_mode-aware fashion.
 864:      * Also, unless sendmail_path points to sendmail (or something that
 865:      * claims to be sendmail), don't pass params (not a perfect fix,
 866:      * but it will do).
 867:      *
 868:      * @param string      $to      To
 869:      * @param string      $subject Subject
 870:      * @param string      $body    Message Body
 871:      * @param string      $header  Additional Header(s)
 872:      * @param string|null $params  Params
 873:      *
 874:      * @return bool
 875:      */
 876:     private function mailPassthru($to, $subject, $body, $header, $params)
 877:     {
 878:         //Check overloading of mail function to avoid double-encoding
 879:         // phpcs:ignore PHPCompatibility.IniDirectives.RemovedIniDirectives.mbstring_func_overloadDeprecatedRemoved
 880:         if ((int)ini_get('mbstring.func_overload') & 1) {
 881:             $subject = $this->secureHeader($subject);
 882:         } else {
 883:             $subject = $this->encodeHeader($this->secureHeader($subject));
 884:         }
 885:         //Calling mail() with null params breaks
 886:         $this->edebug('Sending with mail()');
 887:         $this->edebug('Sendmail path: ' . ini_get('sendmail_path'));
 888:         $this->edebug("Envelope sender: {$this->Sender}");
 889:         $this->edebug("To: {$to}");
 890:         $this->edebug("Subject: {$subject}");
 891:         $this->edebug("Headers: {$header}");
 892:         if (!$this->UseSendmailOptions || null === $params) {
 893:             $result = @mail($to, $subject, $body, $header);
 894:         } else {
 895:             $this->edebug("Additional params: {$params}");
 896:             $result = @mail($to, $subject, $body, $header, $params);
 897:         }
 898:         $this->edebug('Result: ' . ($result ? 'true' : 'false'));
 899:         return $result;
 900:     }
 901: 
 902:     /**
 903:      * Output debugging info via a user-defined method.
 904:      * Only generates output if debug output is enabled.
 905:      *
 906:      * @see PHPMailer::$Debugoutput
 907:      * @see PHPMailer::$SMTPDebug
 908:      *
 909:      * @param string $str
 910:      */
 911:     protected function edebug($str)
 912:     {
 913:         if ($this->SMTPDebug <= 0) {
 914:             return;
 915:         }
 916:         //Is this a PSR-3 logger?
 917:         if ($this->Debugoutput instanceof \Psr\Log\LoggerInterface) {
 918:             $this->Debugoutput->debug(rtrim($str, "\r\n"));
 919: 
 920:             return;
 921:         }
 922:         //Avoid clash with built-in function names
 923:         if (is_callable($this->Debugoutput) && !in_array($this->Debugoutput, ['error_log', 'html', 'echo'])) {
 924:             call_user_func($this->Debugoutput, $str, $this->SMTPDebug);
 925: 
 926:             return;
 927:         }
 928:         switch ($this->Debugoutput) {
 929:             case 'error_log':
 930:                 //Don't output, just log
 931:                 /** @noinspection ForgottenDebugOutputInspection */
 932:                 error_log($str);
 933:                 break;
 934:             case 'html':
 935:                 //Cleans up output a bit for a better looking, HTML-safe output
 936:                 echo htmlentities(
 937:                     preg_replace('/[\r\n]+/', '', $str),
 938:                     ENT_QUOTES,
 939:                     'UTF-8'
 940:                 ), "<br>\n";
 941:                 break;
 942:             case 'echo':
 943:             default:
 944:                 //Normalize line breaks
 945:                 $str = preg_replace('/\r\n|\r/m', "\n", $str);
 946:                 echo gmdate('Y-m-d H:i:s'),
 947:                 "\t",
 948:                     //Trim trailing space
 949:                 trim(
 950:                     //Indent for readability, except for trailing break
 951:                     str_replace(
 952:                         "\n",
 953:                         "\n                   \t                  ",
 954:                         trim($str)
 955:                     )
 956:                 ),
 957:                 "\n";
 958:         }
 959:     }

 990: 
 991:     /**
 992:      * Extract sendmail path and parse to deal with known parameters.
 993:      *
 994:      * @param string $sendmailPath The sendmail path as set in php.ini
 995:      *
 996:      * @return string The sendmail path without the known parameters
 997:      */
 998:     private function parseSendmailPath($sendmailPath)
 999:     {
1000:         $sendmailPath = trim((string)$sendmailPath);
1001:         if ($sendmailPath === '') {
1002:             return $sendmailPath;
1003:         }
1004: 
1005:         $parts = preg_split('/\s+/', $sendmailPath);
1006:         if (empty($parts)) {
1007:             return $sendmailPath;
1008:         }
1009: 
1010:         $command = array_shift($parts);
1011:         $remainder = [];
1012: 
1013:         // Parse only -t, -i, -oi and -f parameters.
1014:         for ($i = 0; $i < count($parts); ++$i) {
1015:             $part = $parts[$i];
1016:             if (preg_match('/^-(i|oi|t)$/', $part, $matches)) {
1017:                 continue;
1018:             }
1019:             if (preg_match('/^-f(.*)$/', $part, $matches)) {
1020:                 $address = $matches[1];
1021:                 if ($address === '' && isset($parts[$i + 1]) && strpos($parts[$i + 1], '-') !== 0) {
1022:                     $address = $parts[++$i];
1023:                 }
1024:                 $this->Sender = $address;
1025:                 continue;
1026:             }
1027: 
1028:             $remainder[] = $part;
1029:         }
1030: 
1031:         // The params that are not parsed are added back to the command.
1032:         if (!empty($remainder)) {
1033:             $command .= ' ' . implode(' ', $remainder);
1034:         }
1035: 
1036:         return $command;
1037:     }
1038:

1040:      * Send messages using $Sendmail.
1041:      */

1043:     {
1044:         $ini_sendmail_path = ini_get('sendmail_path');
1045: 
1046:         if (false === stripos($ini_sendmail_path, 'sendmail')) {
1047:             $ini_sendmail_path = '/usr/sbin/sendmail';
1048:         }
1049:         $this->Sendmail = $this->parseSendmailPath($ini_sendmail_path);
1050:         $this->Mailer = 'sendmail';
1051:     }

1065:     }
